messages.subject: Re: Initialising stochastic nodes with capture-mark-recapture data
messages.subject_clean: Initialising stochastic nodes with capture-mark-recapture data
messages.body_plain:
Just as a final note on this problem in case it is of use to anyone else.... the problem ending up being in the initial values that I was supplying.  The inits that were being chosen from a distruibution were resulting in a survival probability of virtually zero for a node that was knwon to be 1 which was then casuing the error.  With appropriate init values selected (rather than from a distribution) the model runs fine... and fast!  So thanks to all developers for the development and ongoing supprt.  Many thanks.

On Tuesday, 28 January 2020 09:57:01 UTC, Dave Hudson wrote:
> Hi Perry,
>
> Still having trouble with the various warnings when using the more complicated model and I am wondering whether it is an issue of identifiability, I have been using a very simplified data set to try and debug the code as you will see below....
> Basically it is looking at mortality using the Siler function which describes age specific mortality through 5 parameters (a1,a2,b1,b2,c - and c has its lower bound which is dependent on some of the other parameters).  This code has worked in WinBUGS but it takes a long time!
> Any thoughts would be very gratefully received!
>
> Many thanks
> Dave
>
> #Set up matrices for capture history, known latent states, initial latent states and age (3 individuals, 6 time occasions)
> Tch<- matrix(data = NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 6)
> Tch[1,]<- c(1,1,0,1,0,0)
> Tch[2,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,1)
> Tch[3,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,0)
>
> Tknown <- Tch
> Tknown[1,]<- c(1,1,1,1,NA,NA)
> Tknown[2,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
> Tknown[3,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,NA)
>
> Tinit<- Tch
> Tinit[1,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
> Tinit[2,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
> Tinit[3,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,NA)
>
> Tage<- Tch
> Tage[1,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
> Tage[2,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
> Tage[3,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
>
> Tf<- c(1,1,1)
>
> CJS.code<- nimbleCode({
>       # CJS Siler model with constrained C parameter for NIMBLE:
>       # Priors and constraints
>     for (i in 1:nind){
>       for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
>         phi[i,t] <- exp((exp(a1)/b1)*(exp(-b1*x[i,t])-1) - c*x[i,t] + (exp(a2)/b2)*(1-exp(b2*x[i,t])))
>         p[i,t] <- mean.p
>       } #t
>     } #i
>
>     cl <- -exp(a1-(b1*xl)) - exp(a2-(b2*xl)) #Constrain c parameter
>     xl <- (log(b1)+a1-log(b2)-a2)/(b1+b2)    #Constrain c parameter
>
>     a1 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
>     b1 ~ dexp(0.1)
>     a2 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
>     b2 ~ dexp(0.1)
>     c ~ dunif(cl,10)
>     mean.p ~ dunif(0,1)
>
>       # Likelihood
>     for (i in 1:nind){
>       # Define latent state at first capture
>       z[i,f[i]] <- 1
>       for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
>         # State process
>         z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
>         mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]
>         # Observation process
>         y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
>         mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]
>       } #t
>     } #i
>   })
>
> CJS.Consts <- list(f=Tf, nind=3, n.occasions=6, x=Tage)
> CJS.data <- list(y=Tch, z=Tknown)
> CJS.inits <- list(
>   z = Tinit,
>   a1 = rnorm(1),
>   a2 = rnorm(1),
>   b1 = rexp(1, 0.1),
>   b2 = rexp(1, 0.1),
>   mean.p = runif(1,0,1),
>   c = runif(1,1,10)
> )
>
> CJS<- nimbleModel(code=CJS.code, name = "CJS", constants = CJS.Consts,
>                   data = CJS.data, inits = CJS.inits)
>
> spec <- configureMCMC(CJS)
> spec$printSamplers()
>
> rMCMC<- buildMCMC(spec)
>
> cCJS<- compileNimble(CJS)
> cMCMC<- compileNimble(rCJS, project = CJS)
>
> set.seed(0)
> cMCMC$run(1000)
>
>
>
>
> On Friday, 24 January 2020 17:14:22 UTC, pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Dave,
> >
> > That's correct: One variable can contain data nodes and non-data nodes.  When providing data values for a variable, entries for the non-data elements should be NA.  One can then provide inits for the non-data elements. That's all similar to JAGS.
> >
> > When initial values are not provided, they are drawn from their prior.  In your case, the data nodes for some x[i,] will be a series of 1s.  My point about the initial value for the first non-data node after the last 1 (i.e. after the time of last capture) is that you should at least get a valid value whether you make it 0 (the individual died), 1 (the individual survived) or NA (initial 0 or 1 will be drawn based on the survival probability).
> >
> > One reason to provide a 0 or a 1 instead of an NA as inits is that using NA will trigger the warning that the model is not fully initialized (because it's not, which isn't necessarily a bad thing).  Another strategy is you can do model$simulate() to generate values everywhere, then model$calculate().  If the latter returns NA or -Inf, something is still not validly initialized.  As noted in the error message, having a not-fully-initialized model is not a bug or necessarily a problem.  The MCMC (or other algorithm, but I assume you are going for MCMC) might successfully initialize it.
> >
> > The process for determining where you have some invalid initial value in the more complex model would be similar to what we've discussed so far.  You can control which parts of the model are calculated and you can look directly at variables and their associated log probability values, so the process is essentially one of digging around.  The steps are roughly as follows:
> >
> > If model$calculate() is -Inf, try checking different parts of the model to see where something has log probability of -Inf.
> >
> > e.g., model$calculate('z') will calculate the sum of log probabilities for all the z's.  model$calculate('z[1,]') will calculate for just z[1,],  etc.
> >
> > When you have it narrowed down, such as if model$calculate('z') is -Inf, you can also look directly as each node's log probability with model$logProb_z
> >
> > Then you can inspect values relevant to the calculation, e.g. inspect
> > model$z[1,]
> > model$phi[1,]
> > model$mu1
> > etc.
> > Usually this reveals values that result in a -Inf log probability, such as if a parameter to a distribution does not make sense.
> >
> > HTH.  If you're still stuck, please send a reproducible example of the more complex model.
> > -Perry
> >
> > On Thu, Jan 23, 2020 at 10:36 AM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Perry,
> > > Thanks so much for your explanations yesterday, I have been trying to work through this all day today!
> > > Just want to check my understanding... in your explanation you suggest I include a matrix for known x(latent states  (1=known alive, 0=known dead, NA=unknown)) in data, and then also set up the init_x (any known state is left as NA but then any unknown state can be 0,1 or NA...so essentially all of the init_x could just be a matrix of NAs??  So so I need to give the init_x??
> > >
> > > Also, in my own model I am trying to include time varying covariates which means that I need the additional [i,t] notation on my phi and p which then changes my likelihood calculation but this seems to throw similar errors and I cant work out where they are stemming from!!  Below is the likelihood that worked in BUGS... can you see any obvious issues??  Will keep playing around with it!
> > >
> > >       # Likelihood
> > >     for (i in 1:nind){
> > >       # Define latent state at first capture
> > >       z[i,f[i]] <- 1
> > >       for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
> > >         # State process
> > >         z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
> > >         mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]
> > >         # Observation process
> > >         y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
> > >         mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]
> > >       } #t
> > >     } #i
> > >   })
> > >
> > > Many thanks,
> > > Dave
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, 22 January 2020 19:17:40 UTC, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > Actually, what I think you want to do is set x[1,] as *data* equal to 1 1 1 1 1 1 NA. Then the MCMC will not spin its wheels trying to update the first six states because they are essentially known to be 1.  The NA "missing data" means that element will be sampled.  Then I think you want to set x_init [1,] to NA NA NA NA NA NA [0 or 1 or NA].  The first six NAs are because you don't want to provide initial values for non-missing data nodes.  The last value could be 0, or 1, or NA (will be simulated from the prior).  Often in nimble it is a good idea to proactively provide good initial values instead of relying on draws from priors, but in this case it might not matter much.
> > > >
> > > > In my previous answer I was focused on untangling the confusion about valid states and so was not thinking of the way you can set some unobserved states as de facto data in a model like this.
> > > >
> > > > -Perry
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, Jan 22, 2020 at 11:10 AM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thank you both so much... yes, obvious now! I was confusing what x_init was representing. The only thing that still is unclear to me is what the init_x should be when the true unseen state is unknown??  Should this be NA again?  For example, I could have an individual with capture history of y[1,]<- 1 1 1 0 1 1 0 (So captured 3 consecutive times, then missed, then twice more and then that is it... but the individual is not recovered dead) so then x_init would be x_init[1,] <- 1 1 1 1 1 1 NA ???  The NA representing the fact that we do not what the true underlying state of this individual is at t=7
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for all the assitance,
> > > > >
> > > > > Dave
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wednesday, 22 January 2020 18:04:07 UTC, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > > > I think what is needed for each initial state sequence to be some 1s followed by some 0s (or perhaps just all 1s).  Then there will be no initial states that represent an individual going from dead to alive.  In addition, the 1s in the initial states should extend at least as far in time as the last 1 in the corresponding capture history.  Then there will be no captures of dead individuals.  Initial states that represent dead to alive transitions or captures of dead individuals seem to be the most likely culprits for log probabilities of -Inf from the initial values.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > To use your example:
> > > > > > y[1,] <- 1 1 1 0 1 1 0
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I think a valid sequence of initial values for the alive/dead states would be
> > > > > > and x_init[1,] <- 1 1 1 1 1 1 0
> > > > > > where the last value could alternatively be 1.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > dbern(p) is an alternative to dbin(p, 1)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > -Perry
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Wed, Jan 22, 2020 at 8:12 AM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > Yes, I think this would be because a latent alive/dead history such as:
> > > > > > > x[1, 1:7] = 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Implies that individual #1 was alive at T=1,2,3, then died in time period T=4, then came back to life in time period T=5, which is not possible.  So, that's the cause of that error.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I'm so sorry to not be following, but I'm still not sure what you mean by trying to induce "a missed capture event" ?  Do you perhaps mean one of the observation's one of the y[i,j]'s, should be changed to 0?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Wed, Jan 22, 2020 at 1:36 PM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > In my own capture histories I have a lot of 0's where individuals have not been captured and when I run my model it basically lists a load of warnings (E.g. warning: problem initializing stochastic node x[1, 5]: logProb is -Inf.) for every node where a 1 follows a 0.  I was trying to work out whether it was an issue with my code or how I was inputting the data and initial values and thats why I then tried it on the Dipper code which I knew works!  But as soon as there is a missed capture event the warning appears.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks so much for looking into this!
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Wednesday, 22 January 2020 12:25:31 UTC, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Yes, the issue is that when you "Create the missed capture event" as:
> > > > > > > > > x_init[1,4]<-0  #Create the missed capture event
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Then that initial value of x[1,4]=0 is inconsistent with the first row of the observation history:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > head(y)
> > > > > > > > >      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7]
> > > > > > > > > [1,]    1    1    1    1    1    1    0
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Specifically, that y[1,4] = 1.  So x[1,4]=0 is an impossible initial value, since it can't give rise to the observation that takes place.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What again are you trying to accomplish, by setting x[1,4]=0 ?  There's most likely a different, more correct way of doing it.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Wed, Jan 22, 2020 at 12:44 PM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > The code below creates the exact same error/warning messages that I am getting from my own model, I used your dipper code and dataset to see if I could isolate what was going on...
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## Latent State MCMC for the dipper model
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## load nimble library
> > > > > > > > > > library(nimble)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## load data
> > > > > > > > > > load('../data/dipperData.RData')
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > x_init[1,4]<-0  #Create the missed capture event
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## define hierarchical model
> > > > > > > > > >   code <- nimbleCode({
> > > > > > > > > >   phi ~ dunif(0, 1)
> > > > > > > > > >   p ~ dunif(0, 1)
> > > > > > > > > >   for (i in 1:nind) {
> > > > > > > > > >     x[i, first[i]] <- 1
> > > > > > > > > >     for (t in (first[i] + 1):k) {
> > > > > > > > > >       mu_x[i, t] <- phi * x[i, t-1]
> > > > > > > > > >       mu_y[i, t] <- p * x[i, t]
> > > > > > > > > >       x[i, t] ~ dbin(mu_x[i, t], 1)
> > > > > > > > > >       y[i, t] ~ dbin(mu_y[i, t], 1)
> > > > > > > > > >     }
> > > > > > > > > >   }
> > > > > > > > > > })
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## define model constants, data, and initial values
> > > > > > > > > > constants <- list(k=k, nind=nind, first=first)
> > > > > > > > > > data <- list(y=y)
> > > > > > > > > > inits <- list(phi=0.6, p=0.9, x=x_init)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## create model object
> > > > > > > > > > Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## specify MCMC algorithm
> > > > > > > > > > spec <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
> > > > > > > > > > spec$printSamplers()
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## build MCMC algorithm
> > > > > > > > > > Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(spec)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## compile model and MCMC
> > > > > > > > > > Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
> > > > > > > > > > Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > ## run MCMC
> > > > > > > > > > set.seed(0)
> > > > > > > > > > Cmcmc$run(10000)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Wednesday, 22 January 2020 11:14:02 UTC, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Would it be possible for you to post a reproducible example?  Yes, you're right, this most likely is an issue with your initial values, as you suggested quite possible for your "x" values.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Wed, Jan 22, 2020 at 12:03 PM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > > > > > > > > I am a new convert to Nimble but I am struggling to transfer some CJS models from BUGS...
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > I have a similar problem to one posted the other day and I am trying to understand what is happening. I am trying to model survival/mortality from an extensive capture-mark-recapture dataset in a fairly simple CJS format, I have the model which runs in BUGS and I have been trying to reconfigure it to work in Nimble with some success but it repeatedly throws warning messages for every node (recapture event) that follows a zero in the capture history... so for example an individual capture history maybe 11101 to describe an individual who was captured on the first three possible occasions then not captured and then finally recaptured on the final occasion.  All seems to work ok but I get a warning saying warning: problem initializing stochastic node x[1, 5]: logProb is -Inf. So I am wondering waht is happening to throw this warning.  I think it is to do with my x_init values but not quite sure what they should in this situation.  I also tried this with the dipper model from Turek 2016 and had the same warning when I changed an individual's capture history to include a missed capture event.
> > > > > > > > > > > > I can add examples if need be but I think I am missing something simple!?
> > > > > > > > > > > > Many thanks,
> > > > > > > > > > > > Dave

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the follow-up explanation, Dave.

On Wed, Feb 5, 2020 at 1:46 AM Dave Hudson <davehu...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> Just as a final note on this problem in case it is of use to anyone else.... the problem ending up being in the initial values that I was supplying.  The inits that were being chosen from a distruibution were resulting in a survival probability of virtually zero for a node that was knwon to be 1 which was then casuing the error.  With appropriate init values selected (rather than from a distribution) the model runs fine... and fast!  So thanks to all developers for the development and ongoing supprt.  Many thanks.
>
> On Tuesday, 28 January 2020 09:57:01 UTC, Dave Hudson wrote:
> > Hi Perry,
> >
> > Still having trouble with the various warnings when using the more complicated model and I am wondering whether it is an issue of identifiability, I have been using a very simplified data set to try and debug the code as you will see below....
> > Basically it is looking at mortality using the Siler function which describes age specific mortality through 5 parameters (a1,a2,b1,b2,c - and c has its lower bound which is dependent on some of the other parameters).  This code has worked in WinBUGS but it takes a long time!
> > Any thoughts would be very gratefully received!
> >
> > Many thanks
> > Dave
> >
> > #Set up matrices for capture history, known latent states, initial latent states and age (3 individuals, 6 time occasions)
> > Tch<- matrix(data = NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 6)
> > Tch[1,]<- c(1,1,0,1,0,0)
> > Tch[2,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,1)
> > Tch[3,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,0)
> >
> > Tknown <- Tch
> > Tknown[1,]<- c(1,1,1,1,NA,NA)
> > Tknown[2,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
> > Tknown[3,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,NA)

> > > Hi Dave,
> > >
> > > That's correct: One variable can contain data nodes and non-data nodes.  When providing data values for a variable, entries for the non-data elements should be NA.  One can then provide inits for the non-data elements. That's all similar to JAGS.
> > >
> > > When initial values are not provided, they are drawn from their prior.  In your case, the data nodes for some x[i,] will be a series of 1s.  My point about the initial value for the first non-data node after the last 1 (i.e. after the time of last capture) is that you should at least get a valid value whether you make it 0 (the individual died), 1 (the individual survived) or NA (initial 0 or 1 will be drawn based on the survival probability).
> > >
> > > One reason to provide a 0 or a 1 instead of an NA as inits is that using NA will trigger the warning that the model is not fully initialized (because it's not, which isn't necessarily a bad thing).  Another strategy is you can do model$simulate() to generate values everywhere, then model$calculate().  If the latter returns NA or -Inf, something is still not validly initialized.  As noted in the error message, having a not-fully-initialized model is not a bug or necessarily a problem.  The MCMC (or other algorithm, but I assume you are going for MCMC) might successfully initialize it.
> > >
> > > The process for determining where you have some invalid initial value in the more complex model would be similar to what we've discussed so far.  You can control which parts of the model are calculated and you can look directly at variables and their associated log probability values, so the process is essentially one of digging around.  The steps are roughly as follows:
> > >
> > > If model$calculate() is -Inf, try checking different parts of the model to see where something has log probability of -Inf.
> > >
> > > e.g., model$calculate('z') will calculate the sum of log probabilities for all the z's.  model$calculate('z[1,]') will calculate for just z[1,],  etc.
> > >
> > > When you have it narrowed down, such as if model$calculate('z') is -Inf, you can also look directly as each node's log probability with model$logProb_z
> > >
> > > Then you can inspect values relevant to the calculation, e.g. inspect
> > > model$z[1,]
> > > model$phi[1,]
> > > model$mu1
> > > etc.
> > > Usually this reveals values that result in a -Inf log probability, such as if a parameter to a distribution does not make sense.

> > > HTH.  If you're still stuck, please send a reproducible example of the more complex model.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm doing some out-of-sample predictions,
but the posterior summaries of the parameters of interest (the main parameters in the model),
when I consider the calculation of the predicted values inside nimble,
are changing as well.
In WinBUGS we add the option of using the "cut()" function. I'm aware that this is not possible in nimble.
What is the best approach of doing this?

thanks in advance
Rui

messages.subject: Re: out of sample predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rui,

We don't provide a cut() function. In part this is because it's unclear what the posterior is when one uses such functionality (please see Plummer, M. (2015). Cuts in Bayesian graphical models. Statistics and Computing, 25(1), 37-43.)

In general the posterior when running the model with the predicted values (i.e., predictive nodes) and without them should be equivalent, statistically but because you also sample the predictive nodes in the latter case (which shifts which random numbers are being used to sample the parameters), the exact numerical values in the two cases won't be the same. If you're seeing that the posteriors are not equivalent then something is wrong and we could discuss further.

So I think you have two options:

a) Include the predictive nodes in the model and sample as part of the primary MCMC. The downside to this is that the MCMC spends time sampling the predictive nodes, which if you are going to thin your samples anyway (e.g., to save storage space), means you spend time getting samples you won't use. Also, this could affect mixing of the parameters because the parameter updates are done conditional on the values simulated into the predictive nodes. But doing it this way is simplest to manage.

b) Don't include the predictive nodes in the model (or include them but remove the MCMC samplers assigned to them). After you've run the MCMC, you can loop through the iterations, put the parameter values back into the model, and simulate predictive nodes given the parameter values from each of the iterations (or a thinned set of the iterations). To do this, a computationally efficient approach would be to create an expanded model with the additional predictive nodes and write a nimbleFunction that will put parameter values into that expanded model, simulate into the predictive nodes, and store the resulting predictions. A perhaps easier approach to code up quickly is just to do this directly in R via a loop, though for large models this could be slow.  Also note that unless you override it, NIMBLE won't allow simulation into nodes flagged as 'data' nodes, so it's best not to set the predictive nodes to be flagged as 'data'.

> Hi Rui,
>
> We don't provide a cut() function. In part this is because it's unclear what the posterior is when one uses such functionality (please see Plummer, M. (2015). Cuts in Bayesian graphical models. Statistics and Computing, 25(1), 37-43.)
>
> In general the posterior when running the model with the predicted values (i.e., predictive nodes) and without them should be equivalent, statistically but because you also sample the predictive nodes in the latter case (which shifts which random numbers are being used to sample the parameters), the exact numerical values in the two cases won't be the same. If you're seeing that the posteriors are not equivalent then something is wrong and we could discuss further.
>
> So I think you have two options:
>
> a) Include the predictive nodes in the model and sample as part of the primary MCMC. The downside to this is that the MCMC spends time sampling the predictive nodes, which if you are going to thin your samples anyway (e.g., to save storage space), means you spend time getting samples you won't use. Also, this could affect mixing of the parameters because the parameter updates are done conditional on the values simulated into the predictive nodes. But doing it this way is simplest to manage.
>
> b) Don't include the predictive nodes in the model (or include them but remove the MCMC samplers assigned to them). After you've run the MCMC, you can loop through the iterations, put the parameter values back into the model, and simulate predictive nodes given the parameter values from each of the iterations (or a thinned set of the iterations). To do this, a computationally efficient approach would be to create an expanded model with the additional predictive nodes and write a nimbleFunction that will put parameter values into that expanded model, simulate into the predictive nodes, and store the resulting predictions. A perhaps easier approach to code up quickly is just to do this directly in R via a loop, though for large models this could be slow.  Also note that unless you override it, NIMBLE won't allow simulation into nodes flagged as 'data' nodes, so it's best not to set the predictive nodes to be flagged as 'data'.

messages.subject: Re: Community Occupancy / Abundance models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Yes, people have been using nimble for multi-species occupancy and abundance models.  We have a paper led by Lauren Ponisio that will be coming out in Ecology & Evolution that includes such cases.  I'll point to the preprint when the journal posts it.  In the meantime, you could take a look at our workshop materials (https://github.com/nimble-training).  The workshop I gave at Vogelwarte might have the most relevant examples: https://github.com/nimble-training/nimble-Vogelwarte-workshop-2018

There might be two issues going on.  nimble should not crash your R session.  One guess it that your model code has declarations accessing elements of variables that don't exist, i.e. using indices that are too big.  (That still shouldn't crash your system, but conceivably it could.)

Separately, it looks like you need to debug initial values.  The message I sent on Jan. 24 on this thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/9PmFGuJCrbg) suggests how to do that.  We should really get more guides like this more easily available to users.  Anyone want to contribute to the project by helping put something like that together?

Beyond that, we'd need to see a minimal reproducible example to figure out what's going on in your case.

HTH
-Perry

#------------------------------------------------------------------
# Custom sampler to update G.true, subject to constraints stemming from G.use
#------------------------------------------------------------------
GSampler <- nimbleFunction(
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    # Defined stuff
    M <- control$M
    J <- control$J
    K2D <- control$K2D
    nlevels <- control$nlevels
    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
  },
  run = function() {
    #Structures for the SCR observation model likelihood
    lam <- model$lam
    lam.cand <- matrix(0,nrow=M,ncol=J)
    G.true <- model$G.true
    ll.y.sight <- rep(0,J)
    ll.y.sight.cand <- rep(0,J)

    #Update first ID covariate, G.true[,1]. Metropolis-Hastings
    swap <- which(model$G.latent[1:M]==1) #can only update currently latent G's
    for(i in 1:length(swap)){
      G.cand <- rcat(1,model$gammaVec[1:nlevels])
      if(G.cand!=model$G.true[swap[i]]){
        #update ll.y
        d2 <- (model$s[swap[i],1]-model$X[1:J,1])^2 + (model$s[swap[i],2]-model$X[1:J,2])^2 #ideally wouldn't need to recalculate this
        lam.cand[swap[i],1:J]<- model$lam0[G.cand]*exp(-d2/(2*model$sigma[G.cand]^2))
        if(model$z[swap[i]]==1){
          ll.y.sight <- dpois(model$y.sight.true[swap[i],],K2D[swap[i],]*lam[swap[i],],log=TRUE)
          ll.y.sight.cand <- dpois(model$y.sight.true[swap[i],],K2D[swap[i],]*lam.cand[swap[i],],log=TRUE)
        }else{
          ll.y.sight <-rep(0,J)
          ll.y.sight.cand <-rep(0,J)
        }
        #update ll.cat <http://ll.cat>
        ll.cat <http://ll.cat> <- dcat(G.true[swap[i]],prob=model$gammaVec[1:nlevels],log=TRUE)
        ll.cat.cand <- dcat(G.cand,prob=model$gammaVec[1:nlevels],log=TRUE)
        prop.for <- model$gammaVec[G.cand]
        prop.back <- model$gammaVec[G.true[swap[i]]]

        #sum log likelihoods and do MH step
        lp_initial <- ll.cat <http://ll.cat>+sum(ll.y.sight)
        lp_proposed <- ll.cat.cand+sum(ll.y.sight.cand)
        log_MH_ratio <- (lp_proposed+log(prop.back)) - (lp_initial+log(prop.for))
        accept <- decide(log_MH_ratio)

        if(accept){
          G.true[swap[i]] <- G.cand
          lam[swap[i],] <- lam.cand[swap[i],]
        }

      }
    }
    #Put stuff back into model
    model$lam <<- lam
    model$G.true <<- G.true

    #update logProb
    model.lp.proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)

    copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
  },
  methods = list( reset = function () {} )
)

#####Nimble Model

NimModel <- nimbleCode({
  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  # priors for detection and augmentation parameters
  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  for(i in 1:nlevels){
      lam0[i]~dunif(0,10)
      sigma[i]~dunif(0,10)
  }
  psi~dunif(0,1)

  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  # dirichlet priors for category/genotype level frequencies
  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  for(k in 1:nlevels){
    alpha[k] <- 1 # parameters
  }
  gammaVec[1:nlevels]~ddirch(alpha[1:nlevels])

  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  # likelihoods
  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  for(i in 1:M) {

    # currently this assumes a rectangular state space
    # could apply some form of the Meredith trick for an irregular state space
    s[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1],xlim[2])
    s[i,2] ~ dunif(ylim[1],ylim[2])
    lam[i,1:J] <- GetDetectionRate(s = s[i,1:2], X = X[1:J,1:2], J=J,
                                   sigma=sigma[G.true[i]], lam0=lam0[G.true[i]], z=z[i],ID=ID[1:n.samp.latent],
                                   G.latent=G.latent[1:M])#ID and G.latent here as a NIMBLE hack
    # Capture model
    # but y.sight.true is latent, requires custom update - see custom IDsampler
    for(j in 1:J) {
      y.sight.true[i,j] ~ dpois(K2D[i,j]*lam[i,j])
    }

    # Model for categorical identity covariates/genotypes (individual by covariate)
    # G.true also requires custom update - see GSampler

    G.true[i]~dcat(gammaVec[1:nlevels])

  }

  # Data augmentation part
  for(i in (n.marked+1):M){
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
  }

  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  #calculate number of unmarked inds captured, and total pop size
  #--------------------------------------------------------------
  n.cap <- Getncap(y.sight.true=y.sight.true[1:M,1:J],z=z[1:M],M=M,J=J,n.marked=n.marked)
  N <- sum(z[1:M])
})# end model

We had another issue involving parallelization recently that might be related.

Can you try providing the Gsampler object itself as the `type` argument to addSampler?

In other words, somewhere you have

Gsampler <- nimbleFunction(...)

Instead of "type = 'Gsampler'", can you try "type = Gsampler".  Thanks.

Also it looks like everything is sourced inside the foreach loop, which is good.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
I found the problem, sorry to waste your time. I saw that other versions of the sampler were working and noticed I had the target set wrong:

target = paste0("G.true[1:","M]")

which I changed to

paste0("G.true[1:",M,"]")

and it works now. I don't know why the original worked not in parallel.

messages.body_plain:
For some reason, NIMBLE knows what "M" should be when not in parallel, but doesn't know what it should be in parallel.

Incorrect sampler assignment:

                  type = "GSampler",control = list(M=M,J=J,K2D=inits.tmp$K2D,nlevels=nlevels),
                  silent = TRUE)
GSampler sampler: G.true[1:M],  M: 250,  J: 81L,  K2D: custom array,  nlevels: 2

Correct sampler assignment:

conf$addSampler(target = paste0("G.true[1:",M,"]"),
                  type = "GSampler",control = list(M=M,J=J,K2D=inits.tmp$K2D,nlevels=nlevels),
                  silent = TRUE)
GSampler sampler: G.true[1:250],  M: 250,  J: 81L,  K2D: custom array,  nlevels: 2

messages.subject: Writing custom samplers
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I am trying to write a custom MCMC sampler in NIMBLE to produce objective priors for N-mixture models, but I am having some errors and trouble understanding NIMBLE's syntax.  My code is  as follows:

library(nimble)

#approximation function
approximation = nimbleFunction(
  run = function(theta0 = double(0), theta= double(0), prev = double(0), c = double(0)){
    returnType(double(0))
    ap = prev + (theta-theta0)*sqrt(c*exp(prev)-2*(1+prev)) + (theta-theta0)^2*(c*exp(prev)-2)/4 + (theta-theta0)^3/6*c*exp(prev)*sqrt(c*exp(prev)-2*(1+prev))/2
    return(ap)
  }
)

#N-mixture likelihood function

myncol = nimbleRcall(function(x=double(2)){}, Rfun = 'ncol', returnType = double(0) )
mynrow = nimbleRcall(function(x=double(2)){}, Rfun = 'nrow', returnType = double(0) )
mycolSums = nimbleRcall(function(x = double(2)){}, Rfun = 'colSums', returnType = double(0) )

Nmixlik = nimbleFunction(
  run= function(y = double(2), p = double(0), lambda = double(0), N = double(1)){
    returnType(double(0))
    T <- myncol(y)
    R <- mynrow(y)
    bin1.aux <- nimMatrix(0, ncol = T, nrow = R)
    f1 <- nimNumeric(R)
    b <- nimMatrix(0, ncol = T, nrow = R )

    for (i in 1:R) {
      f1[i] <- dpois(N[i], lambda)
      for (j in 1:T) bin1.aux[i, j] <- dbinom(y[i, j], N[i], p, log = TRUE)
    }

    for (i in 1:T) {
      b[,i] <-  bin1.aux[,i]+ f1
    }

    return(sum(mycolSums(b)))

  }
)

# M-H for parameter space of p, ie (0,1)
#c =2 and u(0) =1.31
# p is the target

p_OBp_sampler <- nimbleFunction(

  contains = sampler_BASE,

  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control){
    scale <- 0.1
    N <- model[["N"]]
    lambda <- model[["lambda"]]
    y <- model$C
    prevp <- model[["mup"]]
    c <- 2
  },

  run = function(){

    # draw theta from proposal distribtuion
    proposal <- rnorm(1, model[[target]], scale)

    #approximate
    num_app <- approximation(model[[target]], proposal,prevp,c)

    # compute prior fraction
    frac_p <- -(num_app-prevp)

    #log Metropolis Hasting ratio
    log_MH_ratio <- Nmixlik(y,proposal,lambda,N) - Nmixlik(y,model[[target]],lambda,N) + frac_p

    # M-H step- determine whether or not to accept the newly proposed value. Can also use the decide function
    u <- runif(1,0,1)
    if(u < exp(log_MH_ratio)) jump <- TRUE
    else                      jump <- FALSE

      # store proposal into the model
      model[[target]] <<- proposal

      # store value of mup in model
      model[["mup"]] <<- num_app

    # keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent
    if(jump) copy(from = model, to = mvSaved,nodes = c("p", "mup"), row = 1, logProb = FALSE)
    else copy(from = mvSaved, to = model,nodes = c("p", "mup"), row = 1, logProb = FALSE)

  },

  methods = list(reset = function(){})
)

The objective prior that I am trying to implement is not model-based, it depends on the parameter space and has to be computed numerically. The MCMC is a Metropolis-Hasting.  My question is then in writing the sampler, how do I store the values accepted from the Metropolis-Hasting? I am not sure what the arguments of the copy function do. Depending on whether the proposal is accepted or not, I also want to store num_app as this is used in the next iteration of the sampler. How can I do this? I've looked at the example provided in the manual and some examples in this group but there are not many details. Many thanks for explaining.

I've used the above code to change the sampler of p to my custom sampler  for the N-mixture model:

N_mixcode <- nimbleCode( {

  # Priors

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabian,

There are a bunch of things going on here.

I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.

Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.

You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.

In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.

I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.

The best source of ideas for how samplers work is the source code for nimble's built-in samplers.  Here is our basic Metropolis-Hasting sampler: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L146 Unfortunately there is a fair bit of code to accomplish the adaptation (self-tuning of the proposal standard deviation), but the core propose-accept-reject steps are in the run code.

A good way to see what is happening and learn more about nimble is to run the MCMC in R (uncompiled) and use standard R debugging tools.  For example, you can put a browser() in the run code of your sampler and then step through it each time it is called.

I haven't followed exactly where you are stuck, but it's great to see this application.  I hope this helped and let us know more questions.

We haven't advertised widely because we're going to udpate it soon, but we have put some relevant ecology distributions in a package here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleEcology  It includes a dNmixture distribution that might be useful for you.  However, we have a paper coming out showing that in some cases marginalization makes MCMC more efficient and in other cases not.  The dNmixture marginalization can be fairly costly, so it may not be more efficient.

HTH
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hey Perry and Daniel,

Many thanks for the references and help.  The following link is the MCMC algorithm I am trying to implement: https://projecteuclid.org/download/suppdf_1/euclid.ba/1573117290. The MCMC does not rely on any probabilistic model for priors to produce objective priors. In the algorithm, p(theta) is the prior density which is to be evaluated numerically. l(theta) is the likelihood of the model. I've figured that I cannot use functions like getLogProb as this produces the log probabilities of the entire model when I only want the likelihood. I've followed Perry's advice and cleaned up my likelihood function for the basic N-mixture model(see initial enquiry for model description). My likelihood function was not compiling, so I managed to come across the RW_llFunction sampler which allows one to customized likelihoods. My code for my N-mixture  likelihood function  is:

#N-mixture likelihood function
Nmixlik = nimbleFunction(
  setup = function(model) { },
  run= function() {
    y <- model[["C"]]
    p <- model[["p"]]
    lambda <- model[["lambda"]]
    N <- model[["N"]]

    loglik <- sum(dbinom(y,N,p,log = TRUE) + dpois(N, lambda, log = TRUE))
    returnType(double())
    return(loglik)
  }
)

Nmix_llFun <- Nmixlik(Bmodel)
Nmix_llFun$run()

Using this N-mixture likelihood function, my MCMC sampler compiles. My sampler code is as follows:

# M-H for parameter space of p, ie (0,1) with a uniform proposal distribution

#c =2 and u(0) =1.31
# p is the target

p_OBp <- nimbleFunction(
  name = 'P_OBp',
  contains = sampler_BASE,

  # Parameter extracted in the setup code are only extracted once.

  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control){

    c <- 2
    llFunction <- if(!is.null(control$llFunction))  control$llFunction   else stop('p_OBp sampler missing required control argument: llFunction')
    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
  },

  run = function(){

    #browser()
    prev <- model[["mup"]]

    #browser()
    # current value of p
    currentValue <- model[[target]]

    # draw theta from proposal distribtuion

    proposal <- runif(1,0,1)

    #approximate
    num_app <- approximation(currentValue, proposal,prev,c)

    # compute prior fraction
    frac_p <- -(num_app-prev)

    # current Log likelihood
    current_ll <- llFunction$run()

    # store proposal into the model
    model[[target]] <<- proposal

    #proposal log likelihood
    proposed_ll <- llFunction$run()

    #log Metropolis Hasting ratio
    log_MH_ratio <- (proposed_ll - current_ll) + frac_p + (dunif(currentValue, 0,1, log= TRUE) - dunif(proposal,0,1, log = TRUE))

    if(log_MH_ratio == -Inf) {
      nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1)

      jump <- FALSE
    }else {

      # M-H step- determine whether or not to accept the newly proposed value. Can also use the decide function

      #jump <- decide(log_MH_ratio)

      u <- runif(1,0,1)
      if(u < exp(log_MH_ratio)) jump <- TRUE
      else                      jump <- FALSE

      # store value of mup in model to be used in the next iteration depending on whether the proposal is accepted

      model[["mup"]] <<- num_app

      # keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent

      if(jump) copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row=1, nodes = c(calcNodes, "mup"), logProb = TRUE )
      else copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row=1, nodes = c(calcNodes, "mup"), logProb = TRUE )

    }

  },

  methods = list(reset = function(){})
)

Looking at the code of NIMBLE's sampler, I think I understand how they work. The bit that is unclear to be is the copy function. In the nodes argument do I specify which nodes are updated in the MCMC or is it used to select which nodes are updated in terms of logProb? What does the row argument do? Since the priors in this MCMC  don't have a probability function, I would not have any logProb for them.

I've updated this sampler to be used for the p parameter in the N-mixture model by the following steps.
Bconf = configureMCMC(Bmodel)
Bconf$printSamplers() # inspect default samplers
Bconf$removeSampler(c("p")) # remve samplers on priors
Bconf$printSamplers() # inspect that sampler are indeed emoved
Bconf$addSampler(type = 'p_OBp', target = 'p', control = list(llFunction = Nmix_llFun))
Bconf$printSamplers() # check that samplers are correctly assifned
Bmcmc <- buildMCMC(Bconf) ## build the MCMC from the configuration
Bmcmc$run(niter = 10) ## debug by running it uncompiled

. It compiles without any errors when using compileNimble(), but when I compile it in R, I am encountered with warnings of slice sampler has reached its maximum number of contractions for a number of nodes for N.  Slice samplers were assigned to each node for N by default. In my sampler code, are the values accepted updated in the model? Do you spot any errors?  If p follows a random walk Metropolis-Hasting, there is no error of the maximum number of contractions. Also, Perry mentioned to run the MCMC in R uncompiled, have I done that correctly?  In addition, when I run the model using runMCMC(), I can encounter the error

Run-time size error: expected max(1, max(dim(N)[1L], (dim(y)[1L]) * (dim(y)[2L]))) == max(dim(N)[1L], 1)

I think this probably has to do with how I programmed my likelihood function. Can suggestions as to what is going wrong?

Many thanks for all the help, it has been really helpful.

Fabian

I most certainly can help you with any logistics along the way.  There's a number of things you need to understand and get correct, but it's all very do-able.

> > Hi Fabian,
> >
> > There are a bunch of things going on here.
> >
> > I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.
> >
> > Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.
> >
> > You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.
> >
> > In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.
> >
> > I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.
> >
> > The best source of ideas for how samplers work is the source code for nimble's built-in samplers. messages.subject: spatial mark resight activity center sampler for unmarked individuals
messages.subject_clean: spatial mark resight activity center sampler for unmarked individuals
messages.body_plain:
I recently compared my R-based sampler for various spatial mark resight models to NIMBLE analogs and noticed the point estimates differed slightly. My first intuition is that the activity center sampler chosen by NIMBLE was not adequate and I'm very confident that is the case. I'm wondering if there is a good solution.

In the spatial mark resight scenario I am considering, a known subset of the population of N individuals is marked so that we can identify them upon capture. So the population is divided into a marked component of known size and an unknown component of unknown size. The marked individuals are generally treated the same as in a regular spatial capture-recapture problem and the unmarked samples can be treated in one of two ways. First, we can use the likelihood for the unmarked capture history summed over individuals (we don't know which samples belong to which individuals). Second, we can probabilistically reconstruct the unmarked individual capture history. This second option is generally unnecessary, but the first option cannot be used when you have samples where you cannot tell what their marked status is (could belong to marked or unmarked individuals). Further, when you have samples that you know are from marked individuals, but you don't know which one, the marked individual capture history needs to be probabilistically reconstructed.

Focusing on the unmarked individuals here, on each iteration of the MCMC algorithm, the individual each sample is associated with is proposed to change--samples are being probabilistically reallocated among the M activity centers. So sometimes one specific activity center is allocated 1 or more samples, and sometimes it is not. This makes tuning the activity center sampler difficult. If you use an adaptive tuning, it is largely tuned for when an activity center is allocated 0 samples, because this is the most common state when M is adequate. But then, when a sample is allocated to the activity center, the RW step is too large and it tends to not move. This prevents the activity centers from adjusting once they are allocated a sample.

The problem described above causes convergence to sometimes be extremely slow and the acceptance rates for the activity centers look good because they largely reflect the acceptance rates when no samples are assigned to an activity center. Therefore, the problem is difficult for the naive user to diagnose.

In my R-based sampler, I have just been using my intuition to set a single acceptance rate and it converges relatively quickly. I can replace the NIMBLE-selected sampler with the same sampler I use in R, but the average user will not know what to set the proposal parameter to for their data set. I'm wondering if there is a more foolproof solution for NIMBLE that will automatically select settings that will work for this model. Ideally, we would have an algorithm that will tune the activity center acceptance rates for condition 1 - s[i] is allocated 1 or more samples, condition 2 - s[i] is allocated 0 samples and z[i]=1, and condition 3, is allocated 0 samples and z[i]=0.

You can see the behavior in the attached files. In "smix1", you see the behavior we want. The activity center (just the x dimension plotted here) moves randomly around the state space until a sample is allocated to it, then it explores a very small area of the state space because it is linked to a specific trap. Then eventually, the sample moves to another activity center and so on. In "smix2", you can see a few places where the s[i] sampler gets stuck. Here, what happens is that it is more quickly reallocated to another activity center because it cannot move and better adjust it's position relative to the sample allocated to it.

Any thoughts on a NIMBLE sampler we can use that does not require the user to set a single proposal parameter that is appropriate for each data set? The sampler below works fine (I got it from Nathan Hostetter), but the user must set the proposal parameter appropriately.

myActivityCenterSampler <- nimbleFunction(
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    # Defined stuff
    ind<-control$ind     # defined during the model call. probably a more elegant way to do this, but it works for now.
    scale<-0.50          # could make this adaptive (see examples at nimble's Git)
    xlim<-model$xlim
    ylim<-model$ylim
    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
  },

  run = function() {
    # grab current value of z
    z.curr <- model$z[ind]

    ## If z==0 propose activity center and accept with probablity 1.0
    if(z.curr==0){

      # store proposal into model
      model$s[ind, 1:2] <<- c(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2]))

      # update dependencies
      model$calculate(calcNodes)

      # Accept candidate trajectory with probabliy 1.0 and keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent
      copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

    }#if z.curr==0

    ## If z==1 propose activity center and use MH update to accept/reject
    if(z.curr==1){

      # initial model logProb
      model_lp_initial <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)

      # generate candidate trajectory conditional on current trajectory
      ## this could be more efficient, including adapting the proposal scale parameter
      ## see nimble examples on Git

      # store proposal into model
      #truncated normal
      sx <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(xlim[1], model$s[ind, 1], sd=scale), pnorm(xlim[2], model$s[ind, 1], sd=scale)), model$s[ind, 1], sd=scale)
      sy <- qnorm(runif(1, pnorm(ylim[1], model$s[ind, 2], sd=scale), pnorm(ylim[2], model$s[ind, 2], sd=scale)), model$s[ind, 2], sd=scale)
      model$s[ind, 1:2] <<- c(sx, sy)

      # proposal could be anything, as long as non-symmetric proposals are accounted for in the MH step.
      #model$s[ind, 1:2] <<- c(runif(1, xlim[1], xlim[2]), runif(1, ylim[1], ylim[2]))

      # proposal model logProb
      model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)

      # log-Metropolis-Hastings ratio
      log_MH_ratio <- model_lp_proposed - model_lp_initial
      # Metropolis-Hastings step: determine whether or
      # not to accept the newly proposed value
      accept <- decide(log_MH_ratio)
      if(accept) {
        copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
      } else {
        copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
      }
    }#z==1

  },
  methods = list( reset = function () {} )
)

messages.body_plain:
Here are two common ways to do it.

Nested indexing:
log(lambda[i, k]) <- beta0[k, year[i] ] + <other effects>

where beta0 has three columns, and year is a vector of 1s, 2s, and 3s indicating which year  site i is from.  (You might have data from each site in each year, but in that case nsite must really be number of sites x number of years?)

0/1 Indicators for years 2 and 3:
log(lambda[i, k]) <- beta0[k] + beta1[k] * year2indicator[i] + beta2[k] * year3indicator[i]

where year2indicator[i] is 1 for year 2 data and 0 otherwise, and year3indicator is 1 for year 3 and 0 otherwise.  Then year 1 has intercept beta0, year 2 has intercept beta0+beta1, and year3 has intercept beta0 + beta2.

HTH
Perry

I don't see the call to nimbleMCMC() that you're using, but my strong suspicion is that you're requesting summary=TRUE, for the posterior summary statistics, and further that the sampling of one or more model dimensions is not getting started correctly - my guess is due to bad initial values, or NA's somewhere in your model.  Anyway, I think the posterior samples contain NA's (probably), and then for determining the 95% BCI for the posterior summary statistics, R's quantile() function is complaining about the NA's.

I'd suggest you get the *samples* returned, which is the default (unless you use samples=FALSE), then look at the posterior samples, find which variable(s) have NA's (most likely), then that will point you toward what part(s) of the model are not sampling properly.

Make sense?

messages.subject: Re: pmax on stochastic nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jóhannes,

Thanks for sending the code.  Well, it is simple, but seeing the code allowed me to see that.

It looks like you want max (and in some places min) of scalars.  For that purpose, the functions to use are simply max(a, b) and min(a, b).

pmax and pmin are for vectors, giving component-wise max or min.  nimble attempts to mimic R syntax to a large extent, including in this distinction between pmax/pmin and max/min.  However, nimble is stricter in types, so you'll only want to use pmax and pmin when you really need the component-wise operation for vectors, not for scalars.  In R, a scalar is just a vector of length 1, so this is sometimes the most confusing distinction between nimble's static types (for C++ compilation purposes) and R's dynamic types.

There was a follow-on issue that your example revealed to us, which is that pmax and pmin actually do not work in model code!  But they should.  It should be possible to declare
c[1:N] <- pmax(a[1:N], b[1:N])
but that currently does not work.  It appears that 'pmax' and 'pmin' were simply inadvertently omitted from a list of valid function names for model code used for error-trapping purposes, although they are supported for nimbleFunction compilation.  In other words, they work except that they are error-trapped in models when they don't need to be.  We'll get that modified on our development branch on github and into the next release.  But anyway, yours wasn't really a vector case as far as I could tell.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Writing custom samplers
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabian,

We had some off-list discussion of this, and now I want to reply on list for anyone else interested in this thread.

model$getLogProb(myNodes) will return the sum of cached logProb values for any stochastic nodes in myNodes.  The default for myNodes is the entire model.

To explain a little more, relevant also to the nimCopy question, each stochastic node has an associated log probability density (logProb) value.  The model is like a machine you control.  model$calculate(myNodes) will calculate myNodes in order.  For stochastic nodes, that means it will calculate and store the logProb value.  We refer to the stored logProb values as being cached.  It will also return the sum of the logProb values of the stochastic nodes in myNodes.  model$getLogProb(myNodes) returns the sum of logProbs for the same nodes, but it does not actually calculate them.  It just uses the cached values, which typically were stored by the most recent call to model$calculate(myNodes).  For MCMC sampler purposes, usually the logProbs for the "current" state can be accessed by model$getLogProb, while those for the "proposed" state need to be calculated by model$calculate; see more below.

I haven't had time to go over the paper you linked to.  Typically, a good design for a new prior is to write it as a nimbleFunction provided as a user-defined distribution (User Manual, Ch. 12).  You can have that return any value that you want to be used as a "logProb", even if it is not actually a log probability density.  However, if it is not so simple, then what you are doing could be a good design.  It looks like the 'approximation' function needs both the proposed and current values, in which case a user-defined distribution would not be adequate, and building the prior logic into the sampler is a fine solution.

It looks like you are doing log probability calculations outside of the model, which is not ideal.  I am not 100% sure but I think a possibly better design would be the following:

Make N-mixture likelihood a user-defined distribution for the counts (similar to the code for Ponisio et al. that I sent on this list recently, and similar to what our updated nimbleEcology package will have).  You would have something like
counts[i, 1:T] ~ dNmixture(<various parameters>)
if counts[i, 1:T] are say the counts from T sampling occasions at site i.

I assume that p is what you want to custom sample and that it will be a parameter of your dNmixture distribution.

Then in the custom sampler, setup code would have "calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)" and run code would use "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)" to access the sum of logProbs currently in the model (without the cost of calculating them).  After you put the proposal value of p in the model, "model$calculate(calcNodes)" would return the sum of logProbs with the proposal value of p.

mvSaved is a modelValues object with values for all model nodes and logProbs (which exist only for stochastic nodes).  modelValues is a class for storing multiple sets of values of multiple model variables. For example, mcmc samples are stored in a modelValues object.  Each set of values is called a "row" because we often think of MCMC samples with rows for iterations and columns for nodes. In the case of mvSaved, it needs only one row.  A sampler can assume upon entry that mvSaved and the model are in sync, meaning they have all the same values.  Upon exit, a sampler must leave mvSaved and the model in sync again, possibly with new values as a result of the sampler's update.  When we say mvSaved, we mean the one and only row of mvSaved, since it only needs and only has one row.  During a typical sampler's run steps, it will put some proposal value(s) in the model and call model$calculate.  At this point, mvSaved will be out of sync with model.  If the proposal is to be accepted, typically one copies from the model (which still has the proposal and results of model$calculate) to mvSaved.  If the proposal is to be rejected, typically one copies from mvSaved to the model.

Your first use of nimCopy should include calcNodes because other nodes will not have been modified.  Only nodes modified by model$calculate need to be copied.  In your case, I'm not sure any nodes are modified by llFunction$run(), but if you make use of the model instead of going around it (which is ok, but nonstandard), then you'll have something that needs copying.  But also I don't think you need the log_MH_ratio == -Inf clause at all, because if that is true then the result of decide() later should be 0 (FALSE).  In built-in samplers that you might be looking at, we typically have a step of checking for a -Inf, but typically this is only for the logProb(s) of the target node(s), i.e. their priors.  We check that before calculating dependencies because if a proposal steps outside of valid values for the target, for example, we can reject without calculating everything else.  The later nimCopys look fine, except that they aren't necessary because I think you aren't (yet) using the model in any way except for modifying the target node.  If you are able to re-arrange as suggest above, then you'll have more meaningful copying to do.  What I can't tell from the code is whether this non-standard scheme will mess up other samplers, for example samplers on values of N that might depend on calculations based on p, which would not have been updated in mvSamples upon exit of your sampler, thereby violating the rules for new sampers.

A good strategy for understanding the system is to run *uncompiled*.  Everything will work uncompiled, in which case execution is in pure R.  That means for example that you can put a browser() in the run code of your custom sampler and study the state of the model or whatever else is of interest.  You can access values of the model and modelValues in typical R syntax, covered in the User Manual.  You can also call nimCopy or do other steps directly from the command line if you need to study how they work by experiment.

I'm not sure of how "mup" fits in the graph (model), but ideally what one wants is to have everything logically in the model and then let algorithms use model-generic programming (for example determining relevant nodes by model$getDependencies) to use every model correctly.  So we try to avoid work-arounds like c(calcNodes, "mup"), but they are perfectly fine if you know what you are doing and this one case is all you want to work.

I hope that all helps.

-Perry

On Saturday, February 22, 2020 at 12:50:10 AM UTC, pdevalpine wrote:

> Hi Jóhannes,
>
> Thanks for sending the code.  Well, it is simple, but seeing the code allowed me to see that.
>
> It looks like you want max (and in some places min) of scalars.  For that purpose, the functions to use are simply max(a, b) and min(a, b).
>
> pmax and pmin are for vectors, giving component-wise max or min.  nimble attempts to mimic R syntax to a large extent, including in this distinction between pmax/pmin and max/min.  However, nimble is stricter in types, so you'll only want to use pmax and pmin when you really need the component-wise operation for vectors, not for scalars.  In R, a scalar is just a vector of length 1, so this is sometimes the most confusing distinction between nimble's static types (for C++ compilation purposes) and R's dynamic types.
>
> There was a follow-on issue that your example revealed to us, which is that pmax and pmin actually do not work in model code!  But they should.  It should be possible to declare
> c[1:N] <- pmax(a[1:N], b[1:N])
> but that currently does not work.  It appears that 'pmax' and 'pmin' were simply inadvertently omitted from a list of valid function names for model code used for error-trapping purposes, although they are supported for nimbleFunction compilation.  In other words, they work except that they are error-trapped in models when they don't need to be.  We'll get that modified on our development branch on github and into the next release.  But anyway, yours wasn't really a vector case as far as I could tell.
>
> -Perry
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben, thanks for this report. In this case, we should be error
trapping when a user gives the target for sampling as something
involving an index without fully numeric values. As it is now, when we
are resolving what nodes correspond to "G.true[1:M]" we actually
evaluate 1:M as code and pick up "M" by R's scoping rules. I suspect
in the parallel version, the R variable "M" has not been copied over
to the worker environments, though I didn't look in detail at that
question.

I'll file a note for us to make better error trapping for cases like this.

>                   type = "GSampler",control = list(M=M,J=J,K2D=inits.tmp$K2D,nlevels=nlevels),
>                   silent = TRUE)
>
> GSampler sampler: G.true[1:M],  M: 250,  J: 81L,  K2D: custom array,  nlevels: 2
>
>
> Correct sampler assignment:
>

>                   type = "GSampler",control = list(M=M,J=J,K2D=inits.tmp$K2D,nlevels=nlevels),
>                   silent = TRUE)
>
> GSampler sampler: G.true[1:250],  M: 250,  J: 81L,  K2D: custom array,  nlevels: 2
>
>
>

Minor correction: Where I referred to "mvSamples", it should have been "mvSaved", as in the rest of the explanation.

On Sat, Feb 22, 2020 at 2:15 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Fabian,
>
> We had some off-list discussion of this, and now I want to reply on list for anyone else interested in this thread.
>
> model$getLogProb(myNodes) will return the sum of cached logProb values for any stochastic nodes in myNodes.  The default for myNodes is the entire model.
>
> To explain a little more, relevant also to the nimCopy question, each stochastic node has an associated log probability density (logProb) value.  The model is like a machine you control.  model$calculate(myNodes) will calculate myNodes in order.  For stochastic nodes, that means it will calculate and store the logProb value.  We refer to the stored logProb values as being cached.  It will also return the sum of the logProb values of the stochastic nodes in myNodes.  model$getLogProb(myNodes) returns the sum of logProbs for the same nodes, but it does not actually calculate them.  It just uses the cached values, which typically were stored by the most recent call to model$calculate(myNodes).  For MCMC sampler purposes, usually the logProbs for the "current" state can be accessed by model$getLogProb, while those for the "proposed" state need to be calculated by model$calculate; see more below.
>
> I haven't had time to go over the paper you linked to.  Typically, a good design for a new prior is to write it as a nimbleFunction provided as a user-defined distribution (User Manual, Ch. 12).  You can have that return any value that you want to be used as a "logProb", even if it is not actually a log probability density.  However, if it is not so simple, then what you are doing could be a good design.  It looks like the 'approximation' function needs both the proposed and current values, in which case a user-defined distribution would not be adequate, and building the prior logic into the sampler is a fine solution.
>
> It looks like you are doing log probability calculations outside of the model, which is not ideal.  I am not 100% sure but I think a possibly better design would be the following:
>
> Make N-mixture likelihood a user-defined distribution for the counts (similar to the code for Ponisio et al. that I sent on this list recently, and similar to what our updated nimbleEcology package will have).  You would have something like
> counts[i, 1:T] ~ dNmixture(<various parameters>)
> if counts[i, 1:T] are say the counts from T sampling occasions at site i.
>
> I assume that p is what you want to custom sample and that it will be a parameter of your dNmixture distribution.
>
> Then in the custom sampler, setup code would have "calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)" and run code would use "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)" to access the sum of logProbs currently in the model (without the cost of calculating them).  After you put the proposal value of p in the model, "model$calculate(calcNodes)" would return the sum of logProbs with the proposal value of p.
>
> mvSaved is a modelValues object with values for all model nodes and logProbs (which exist only for stochastic nodes).  modelValues is a class for storing multiple sets of values of multiple model variables. For example, mcmc samples are stored in a modelValues object.  Each set of values is called a "row" because we often think of MCMC samples with rows for iterations and columns for nodes. In the case of mvSaved, it needs only one row.  A sampler can assume upon entry that mvSaved and the model are in sync, meaning they have all the same values.  Upon exit, a sampler must leave mvSaved and the model in sync again, possibly with new values as a result of the sampler's update.  When we say mvSaved, we mean the one and only row of mvSaved, since it only needs and only has one row.  During a typical sampler's run steps, it will put some proposal value(s) in the model and call model$calculate.  At this point, mvSaved will be out of sync with model.  If the proposal is to be accepted, typically one copies from the model (which still has the proposal and results of model$calculate) to mvSaved.  If the proposal is to be rejected, typically one copies from mvSaved to the model.
>
> Your first use of nimCopy should include calcNodes because other nodes will not have been modified.  Only nodes modified by model$calculate need to be copied.  In your case, I'm not sure any nodes are modified by llFunction$run(), but if you make use of the model instead of going around it (which is ok, but nonstandard), then you'll have something that needs copying.  But also I don't think you need the log_MH_ratio == -Inf clause at all, because if that is true then the result of decide() later should be 0 (FALSE).  In built-in samplers that you might be looking at, we typically have a step of checking for a -Inf, but typically this is only for the logProb(s) of the target node(s), i.e. their priors.  We check that before calculating dependencies because if a proposal steps outside of valid values for the target, for example, we can reject without calculating everything else.  The later nimCopys look fine, except that they aren't necessary because I think you aren't (yet) using the model in any way except for modifying the target node.  If you are able to re-arrange as suggest above, then you'll have more meaningful copying to do.  What I can't tell from the code is whether this non-standard scheme will mess up other samplers, for example samplers on values of N that might depend on calculations based on p, which would not have been updated in mvSamples upon exit of your sampler, thereby violating the rules for new sampers.
>
> A good strategy for understanding the system is to run *uncompiled*.  Everything will work uncompiled, in which case execution is in pure R.  That means for example that you can put a browser() in the run code of your custom sampler and study the state of the model or whatever else is of interest.  You can access values of the model and modelValues in typical R syntax, covered in the User Manual.  You can also call nimCopy or do other steps directly from the command line if you need to study how they work by experiment.
>
> I'm not sure of how "mup" fits in the graph (model), but ideally what one wants is to have everything logically in the model and then let algorithms use model-generic programming (for example determining relevant nodes by model$getDependencies) to use every model correctly.  So we try to avoid work-arounds like c(calcNodes, "mup"), but they are perfectly fine if you know what you are doing and this one case is all you want to work.
>
> I hope that all helps.
>
> -Perry
